html:
The Battle of Megiddo was fought about 1457 BCE near the city of Megiddo, in the north of today's Israel. The Egyptian pharaoh Thutmose III beat a coalition of Canaanite kings led by the king of Kadesh.

When Thutmose began to rule alone, the cities of Canaan and Syria rose against Egypt, probably with the backing of Mitanni. Their armies gathered at Megiddo, which guarded the main road between Egypt and Mesopotamia. Thutmose marched north and, against his officers' advice, took his army through a narrow pass in single file. He came out close to the city and surprised the rebels, who broke and ran for the walls. The Egyptians stopped to loot the camp, so the city had to be taken by a siege of about seven months.

The victory gave Egypt firm control of Canaan and opened the way for campaigns as far as the Euphrates. It is the first battle in history recorded in some detail, from the annals carved at Karnak. The date is uncertain: older books give 1479 or 1482 BCE. The word Armageddon comes from the name Megiddo.
